text.p: Gabon's prime minister, Paulin Obame Nguema, has offered his transitional government's resignation following municipal and legislative elections under a deal to end political strife in the Central African nation.

The resignation, tendered on Friday, precedes Sunday's first round elections for a senate or upper house of parliament to wrap up a transition in the oil-producing nation agreed under the 1994 Paris Accords.

Since a 1990 national conference which mapped out Gabon's first democratic transition, the government has included members of the opposition but President Omar Bongo's ruling Democratic Party (PDG) won 100 of parliament's 120 seats in December.

The elections are part of a democratic timetable brokered in Paris in 1994 to defuse political violence which shook Gabon after Bongo won a disputed 1993 presidential election. Over a dozen people died in the unrest.

Bongo has ruled the former French colony since 1968 after the death of founding head of state, Leon Mba. Gabon, like other African nations, embarked on democratic reforms after the fall of Soviet-bloc communism.
Opposition leader Father Paul Mba Abessole became mayor of the capital Libreville, after his National Woodcutters' Rally won October's municipal elections there.
The ruling party bounced back in the legislative poll, Gabon's second multi-party national assembly election. It won most seats in Libreville.
Bongo's presidential term ends in 1998. Abessole was runner-up in 1993.
